title: The LLD Interview Framework
summary: A repeatable 9-step method for any LLD interview — from clarifying requirements to defending trade-offs. The playbook that ties the case studies together.

blocks.markdown:
An **LLD (low-level design) interview** asks you to design a system's classes, not its servers — think parking lot, elevator, or rate limiter.

- Interviewers aren't grading your final diagram — they're grading your **process**.
- A repeatable framework stops you from freezing or rambling.
- Same 9 steps work whether the prompt is a parking lot or a chess engine.
- This topic is the method; case studies apply it.

blocks.subTitle: The 9 steps
blocks.markdown:
The full sequence, in order.

| # | Step |
|---|---|
| 1-3 | Clarify → entities → attributes/behaviors |
| 4-6 | Relationships → patterns/SOLID → class diagram |
| 7-9 | APIs → edge cases → trade-offs |

Each step's output feeds the next — skipping one shows up later as rework.

One pass, left to right — each box is a checkpoint, not a detour.

Small caption under the arrows reading 'requirements drive every later step'. 2-3 word labels only. >>>

Notice code doesn't appear until step 7 — structure comes first.

Never design against an assumed spec. Spend the first 3-5 minutes narrowing scope.

- Split into **functional requirements** (what it must do: book a slot, process a payment) and **non-functional requirements** (how well: concurrency, scale, latency).
- Ask: who are the actors? What's in scope vs explicitly out? Single machine or distributed?
- Restate the scope back before moving on — it anchors every later step.

**Entities** are the real-world things your classes will model. Find them with **noun extraction** — read the requirements and underline every noun.

- Repeated, concrete nouns become **candidate classes** (Vehicle, Spot, Ticket).
- Drop nouns that are just attributes of another entity (a "license plate" belongs to Vehicle, it isn't its own class).
- Verbs hint at behaviors you'll assign in step 3.

blocks.subTitle: Noun extraction in practice
blocks.markdown:
Requirement: *"A driver parks a vehicle in a spot and receives a ticket with an entry time."*

```
Nouns:  driver, vehicle, spot, ticket, entry time
Verbs:  parks, receives

Candidate classes:
  Vehicle   -> licensePlate, type
  Spot      -> spotId, isOccupied
  Ticket    -> entryTime, vehicle, spot
```

"Driver" often stays out of v1 — it's not referenced again in behaviors.

For each entity, list what it **knows** (attributes) and what it **does** (behaviors/methods).

- Attributes come from the nouns' properties: Spot knows `spotId`, `isOccupied`.
- Behaviors come from the verbs: Spot can `occupy()`, `vacate()`.
- Keep behavior on the entity that owns the data it touches — this is where **encapsulation** starts paying off.

Decide how entities connect — this shapes your class diagram more than anything else.

- **Association** — objects know about each other, no ownership (Driver uses Ticket).
- **Aggregation** — a whole holds parts that can outlive it (ParkingLot has Spots).
- **Composition** — a whole owns parts that die with it (Ticket owns its Payment).
- **Inheritance** — "is-a" (CompactSpot is-a Spot).

Getting this wrong is the single biggest source of a wobbly diagram.

Only now — after the shape exists — reach for design patterns and [solid-principles](solid-principles).

- Pick a pattern because a **specific pain point** appears (many spot types → Strategy; one lot instance → Singleton), not because you know the pattern.
- Check SOLID as a sanity pass: does one class do too much (SRP)? Can you add a spot type without editing existing code (OCP)?
- If nothing hurts yet, skip patterns — they're a fix, not a decoration.

Put steps 2-5 on paper (or whiteboard) as a **UML class diagram** — boxes for classes, lines for relationships.

- Show only class name, 2-3 key attributes, 2-3 key methods per box — not every field.
- Use UML's own notation for the relationship types from step 4 (filled diamond for composition, open diamond for aggregation, hollow triangle for inheritance).
- This is the artifact interviewers photograph — see [uml-for-interviews](uml-for-interviews).

Turn the important behaviors into concrete **method signatures** — name, parameters, return type.

- Only the methods a caller from outside would use: `ParkingLot.parkVehicle(vehicle): Ticket`, not every private helper.
- State the return type for failure cases too — does it throw, return null, or return an `Optional`?
- This is the first point actual "code" shows up — resist writing full method bodies unless asked.

Senior signal: you raise these before the interviewer has to ask.

- **Edge cases** — lot is full, invalid ticket, double payment, spot already occupied.
- **Concurrency** — two threads grabbing the last spot at once; state which method needs a lock and why.
- Naming the race condition matters more than writing the exact locking code.

Close by defending your design, not just presenting it.

- Name what you optimized for and what you gave up (simplicity vs. flexibility, memory vs. speed).
- Answer "what if" out loud: what changes if we add electric-vehicle spots, or scale to 10 lots?
- A design that can absorb a new requirement with one new class — not a rewrite — is the goal.

The three failures that show up most.

- **Jumping to code** — writing classes before requirements are clear; you build the wrong thing fast.
- **Over-engineering with patterns** — forcing Factory, Observer, and Strategy into a design that didn't ask for them. Interviewers notice pattern-for-pattern's-sake.
- **Ignoring requirements** — solving a general version of the problem instead of the one actually asked.

A typical LLD round is 45 minutes. Rough budget for a mid-size prompt.

| Minutes | Steps |
|---|---|
| 5 | Clarify (1) |
| 20 | Entities → diagram (2-6) |
| 15 | APIs, edge cases (7-8) |
| 5 | Trade-offs (9) |

If you're stuck, say your assumption out loud and keep moving — silence costs more than a wrong guess.

The rubric is rarely "did you get the exact right classes."

- **Process** — did you clarify before designing, and did each step follow from the last?
- **Communication** — did you narrate decisions instead of silently drawing boxes?
- **Judgment** — did you justify a pattern or trade-off instead of naming it and moving on?

A clean but unjustified diagram scores lower than a messier one you can defend.

blocks.subTitle: The overall approach
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Walk me through how you approach an LLD problem.**

Clarify functional and non-functional requirements first, extract entities by noun-picking from the requirements, give each entity attributes and behaviors, map relationships between them, apply patterns only where a real pain point appears, sketch the class diagram, define the public APIs, call out edge cases and concurrency, then discuss trade-offs.

Saying the steps in order, out loud, is itself part of the answer.

blocks.subTitle: Finding the classes
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you find the right classes/entities for a system?**

Read the requirements sentence by sentence and pull out the nouns — those are candidate classes. Keep the ones that recur or carry their own data and behavior; fold the rest into an attribute of another class. Verbs attached to those nouns become methods in the next step.

If two people extract slightly different entities, that's normal — defend the ones you kept.

blocks.subTitle: Choosing patterns
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you decide which design patterns to use?**

Let the requirement create the pain first: multiple interchangeable algorithms points to Strategy, one shared instance points to Singleton, notifying many listeners points to Observer. Never start from "which pattern should I show off" — that produces designs that look clever but don't fit.

Being able to say *why* a pattern applies matters more than naming more of them.

blocks.subTitle: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are the most common LLD interview mistakes?**

Jumping straight to code before requirements are clear, over-engineering with patterns the problem never asked for, and quietly redesigning a bigger system than what was actually requested. All three come from skipping step 1 — clarify first.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional requirements
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you handle non-functional requirements in LLD?**

Ask for them explicitly during clarification — concurrency, expected scale, latency — since they change class design, not just deployment. A thread-safety requirement might turn a plain field into a locked one; a scale requirement might turn a Singleton into a pool. Bake them in early instead of patching them in at the end.
